props.title: The Incredible Mr. Limpet
props.initialSlug: Meek bookkeeper becomes heroic fish in WWII comedy

sections.content: The Incredible Mr. Limpet (1964) stands as a fascinating technical breakthrough in combining live-action and animation, predating similar hybrid experiments like Who Framed Roger Rabbit (1988) by decades. Don Knotts stars as Henry Limpet, a mild-mannered bookkeeper who transforms into an animated fish and helps the U.S. Navy fight German U-boats during WWII. The film's unique underwater sequences pushed the boundaries of what was possible with animation integration in the 1960s, while Warner Bros' animation team, led by veterans of their Looney Tunes division, brought their characteristic style to the aquatic characters.

sections.content: The military-aquatic subgenre that The Incredible Mr. Limpet helped pioneer found surprising resonance in later films like Operation Petticoat (1959) and Down Periscope (1996). While these films took different approaches to combining naval warfare with comedy, Limpet's influence on mixing whimsy with wartime storytelling can't be understated. The film's success also paved the way for more ambitious live-action/animation hybrids like Mary Poppins (1964) and Bedknobs and Broomsticks (1971).

Don Knotts' performance as Henry Limpet established a template for fish-out-of-water transformations that would influence films for decades to come, from Big (1988) to The Little Mermaid (1989). His characteristic nervous energy and earnest delivery helped ground the fantastic elements of the story, making the premise more believable despite its outlandish nature. The film's lasting impact can be seen in modern hybrid features like Space Jam (1996) and Stuart Little (1999). SUBHEAD: Animation Innovation and Technical Achievement

movies.slug: A beautiful Irish animated film about a boy who discovers his sister is a selkie who must return to the sea

sections.content: The film's technical achievements in underwater animation deserve special recognition. The team developed new techniques for rendering underwater effects and creating believable interaction between live actors and animated elements. These innovations influenced later underwater sequences in films like The SpongeBob SquarePants Movie (2004) and Ponyo (2008). The film's unique visual style also helped establish a distinctive look for underwater animation that would influence everything from The Little Mermaid (1989) to Finding Nemo (2003).
